BackOff.message: Back-off restarting failed container coturn in pod app-c-coturn-549854dfcb-jgp4h_app-c-prod(faf3240b-a897-45ce-8aa9-136f745cc344)

tracked_hits.meaning: Container keeps dying and the restart interval grows (CrashLoopBackOff)
Container termination. Mixed with forced kills after terminationGracePeriod it signals missing graceful shutdown

alertmanager_alerts_by_state.why: Alerts held by Alertmanager (active, suppressed). A large suppressed count means silences/inhibitions are swallowing a lot

alertmanager_notifications_failed_1d.why: Notifications Alertmanager failed to deliver to receivers (24h). Anything above 0 means alerts are being lost

alerts_fired_15d.why: Alert names that were firing at least once in 15 days. Compared with the rule list this yields "alerts that never fired"

alerts_firing_now.why: Alerts firing right now (name, severity, namespace)

alerts_firing_samples_7d.why: Top alerts by samples observed firing over 7 days (fatigue). At a 30s evaluation interval one day is 2,880; 20,160 means firing for all 7 days

alerts_firing_stale_days.why: Alerts continuously active (pending or firing) for more than 3 days, and for how many days. Nobody is acting on them

am_cluster_members.why: Alertmanager cluster member count (absent when not HA)

am_notifications_1d.why: Notifications sent per receiver integration (slack, email, ...) in 24h. Non-zero ones are the channels actually in use

am_received_1d.why: Alerts Alertmanager received in 24h (firing, resolved). Many firing and no resolved means alerts that never stop

am_reload_ok.why: Whether the last Alertmanager config reload succeeded

apiserver_401_rate_1h.why: 1h average 401s (authentication failures) per second. A client retrying with an expired token or a wrong kubeconfig

apiserver_429_rate.why: Requests per second the apiserver rejected with 429 (Too Many Requests). Client QPS floods or Priority and Fairness (APF) limits

apiserver_5xx_rate.why: apiserver 5xx per second. etcd trouble, webhook timeouts, overload

apiserver_inflight.why: In-flight requests (mutating, readOnly). At the limit 429s appear

apiserver_p99_latency_by_verb.why: Request p99 latency per verb (excluding WATCH and CONNECT). Above 1s kubectl and controllers slow down

apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis.why: Deprecated APIs still being called (group, version, resource, removal release). Pluto looks at stored objects; this metric looks at calls

apiserver_resource_objects_top.why: Top object counts per group and resource since Kubernetes 1.34 (apiserver_resource_objects, the replacement of apiserver_storage_objects); empty before 1.34, where lib/controlplane.py reads apiserver_storage_objects_top

apiserver_storage_objects_top.why: Top object counts per resource type up to Kubernetes 1.36 (deprecated since 1.34, hidden from 1.37). Piled-up completed Jobs, events and runner pods slow LISTs down

apiserver_storage_size_bytes.why: etcd database size (reported by the apiserver). EKS hides etcd but exposes this metric — the limit is 8GiB

apiserver_top_requests.why: Top requests per second by (resource, verb). apiserver_request_total has no client label, so "who" needs the audit log; "what" is seen here. Traces of a runaway controller or CI

apiserver_watch_count.why: Open WATCH count. Proportional to the number of controllers and agents. A spike is an informer restart storm

apiserver_watch_per_node.why: Open WATCHes per node. Scaling with node count is normal (a few each for kubelet, kube-proxy, CNI). Hundreds means a controller or agent is spawning informers freely

apiserver_webhook_p99_by_name.why: p99 latency per admission webhook. A slow webhook slows every create and update

besteffort_pods.why: List of BestEffort pods (neither request nor limit). Those in production namespaces are evaluated in the first pass

cardinality_top_metrics.why: Top 20 metric names by series count. Hundreds of thousands means a Prometheus memory blow-up

conntrack_ratio.why: Node conntrack table usage. Above 0.8 new connections are silently dropped

container_cpu_request_cores.why: Current container CPU request (cores). Evidence for the ratio checks

container_memory_request_bytes.why: Current container memory request (bytes). Evidence for the ratio checks

coredns_cache_entries.why: Cache entries (by pod and type). Read together with the default memory limit of 170Mi

coredns_cache_hit_ratio_1h.why: Cache hit ratio (1h). When low, upstream round trips grow and spread into latency and SERVFAIL. Input for tuning cache TTL and autopath

coredns_forward_by_upstream_rcode_1h.why: Forwarded queries per upstream (forward target) and rcode (1h). Many NXDOMAINs sent upstream mean ndots noise leaking out; SERVFAIL means an upstream failure

coredns_forward_healthcheck_failures_1h.why: Upstream health check failures (1h). Non-zero means the upstream resolver dies intermittently

coredns_forward_p99_1h.why: Upstream response p99 (seconds). Tells whether a high overall CoreDNS p99 is caused by the upstream

coredns_max_concurrent_rejects_1h.why: Queries rejected by the forward max_concurrent limit (1h). Non-zero means CoreDNS is overloaded

coredns_p50_1h.why: Request p50 (seconds). p99 is in core. A p50 above 10ms means CoreDNS itself is slow

coredns_p99_1h.why: CoreDNS request p99 (seconds, 1h). Near 5s is the UDP conntrack race; above 0.1s is CoreDNS overload or upstream latency

coredns_qps_by_pod.why: Queries per second per pod (5m). Concentration on one pod means UDP conntrack pinning or client cache bias

coredns_reload_failed_1h.why: Corefile reload failures (1h). A bad ConfigMap edit leaves CoreDNS running on the old configuration

coredns_requests_by_type_1h.why: Requests in 1h by record type. In a cluster without IPv6, AAAA equal to A means half of the queries are wasted

coredns_responses_by_rcode_1h.why: Responses in 1h by rcode. A high NXDOMAIN ratio is the noise of external names being queried first with the cluster.local suffixes because of the ndots:5 search path

coredns_rest_client_errors_1h.why: Non-2xx responses from CoreDNS → apiserver calls (1h). If the Service/EndpointSlice watch breaks, new service names stop resolving

coredns_servfail_ratio_1h.why: CoreDNS SERVFAIL ratio (1h). Upstream or plugin trouble. Above 0.01 applications see DNS delays and failures

coredns_up.why: Number of CoreDNS pods being scraped

cpu_limit_p95_ratio_7d.why: Container 7-day CPU p95 usage / limit. Above 0.9 it hits the limit and throttling becomes routine (a leading indicator for cpu-throttling)

cpu_p95_7d_cores.why: Container 7-day CPU p95 absolute value (cores). Evidence number for the ratio checks

cpu_request_p95_ratio_7d.why: Container 7-day CPU p95 usage / request. Below 0.3 is over-allocation (node cost); only requests >= 100m and pods older than 1 day

cpu_throttle_ratio_24h.why: The same ratio over 24 hours, weighted by the periods each hour ran. The 5-minute value says "now", this one says "through the day"; resources.cpu-throttling fails only on this one and warns on a 5-minute spike alone

cpu_throttle_ratio_5m.why: CFS throttling ratio: the share of 100ms periods in which a container with a limit was stalled. Above 0.25 latency spikes (Buffer and Omio postmortems). The usual formula aggregates by (namespace, pod); here it is split down to container, because telling sidecars from app containers is what says which limit to fix. The first-pass evaluation judges this per container as is

disk_usage_ratio.why: Node filesystem usage (root, container data). From 0.85 the kubelet starts image GC and eviction

endpoint_not_ready_addresses.why: Endpoints with not-ready addresses behind a Service (pods failing readiness are out of traffic)

endpoint_ready_addresses.why: Ready address count per Endpoints object (distinct addresses). No check reads it; lib/traffic.py counts ready addresses from the Endpoints objects. Raw evidence next to endpoint_not_ready_addresses

flannel_if_drops_1d.why: RX/TX drops that increased over 24 hours. Unlike the cumulative-since-boot node script, this shows "is it still increasing now"

flannel_if_errors_1d.why: RX/TX errors that increased on flannel.1 and cni0 over 24 hours (by node and device). Non-zero means overlay packets are being corrupted (MTU, underlay NIC)

flannel_if_mtu.why: flannel.1 MTU as seen by node-exporter (cross-check with the node script)

flannel_if_up.why: Whether the flannel.1 interface is up (by node). 0 means that node's pods cannot talk to other nodes

flannel_overlay_bytes_1d.why: Overlay bytes sent and received in 24 hours (by node). Scale of inter-node traffic — a large value means pods are crossing nodes to reach databases and caches

fluentbit_dropped_records_1h.why: Records dropped at the output stage

fluentbit_input_records_1h.why: Log records read in 1h. 0 means the agent has stopped

fluentbit_output_errors_1h.why: Errors from fluent-bit outputs (ES, Loki, CloudWatch) in 1h. Logs are not being written to the store

fluentbit_retries_failed_1h.why: Chunks dropped after retries also failed. Those logs are a permanent gap

hpa_at_max.why: HPAs whose current replicas sit at maxReplicas. They cannot grow further, so scaling is effectively off

hpa_at_max_ratio_15d.why: Share of the last 15 days the current replicas sat at max. Near 1 the HPA has been capped

hpa_at_min_ratio_15d.why: Share of the last 15 days the current replicas sat at min. Above 0.99 with max > min the HPA never moved (wrong target or over-requesting)

hpa_desired_changes_7d.why: How often desired replicas changed in 7 days. Dozens means flapping (up and down in short cycles). Happens without behavior stabilization

hpa_min_max.why: min/max/current per HPA. min==max makes the HPA meaningless; a too-small max blocks at traffic peaks

http_metric_namespaces.why: Namespaces with application-level HTTP/gRPC server metrics (the latency, traffic and error inputs of the 4 golden signals). Without them you depend on ingress/ALB metrics

ingress_controller_requests.why: Ingress controller request metrics (ingress-nginx, Traefik). Per-ingress latency, traffic and errors without app metrics. EKS ALB goes through CloudWatch instead

ingress_nginx_p95_1h.why: 1h p95 response time per ingress-nginx Ingress (seconds)

ingress_nginx_rps_1h.why: 1h average RPS per ingress-nginx Ingress. No series when controller metrics are off (observability.golden-signals-missing)

inode_usage_ratio.why: inode usage. Disk space left but no files can be created. A sign of log file explosion

keda_scaler_errors_24h.why: KEDA scaler (trigger) failures reading external metrics per ScaledObject (24h), KEDA 2.14.0 and later. No series when KEDA is not scraped by Prometheus or older than 2.14

kubelet_pleg_p99_1h.why: kubelet PLEG (pod lifecycle relist) p99 latency per node (1h). Above 3s the node goes NotReady with "PLEG is not healthy"

kubelet_running_pods.why: Pods run by the kubelet per node vs the node pod limit (allocatable pods)

kubeproxy_ct_invalid_dropped_1h.why: Packets dropped in conntrack INVALID state (1h). A sign of asymmetric routing or conntrack table trouble

kubeproxy_iptables_rules.why: iptables rule count per node and table, both IP families added (one series per family since 1.33). Above 10k nat rules syncs slow down; grounds for moving to ipvs/nftables. Absent in ipvs and nftables mode

kubeproxy_last_sync_age_s.why: Seconds since the last sync. On 1.29+ syncs only run on change, so this can grow; informational

kubeproxy_no_local_endpoint_services.why: Services with a Local traffic policy (internal or external) whose endpoints are all off this node, per node and policy, right now. Traffic for such a Service arriving at that node is dropped. The max over the two IP families (one series each since 1.33) is a lower bound of distinct Services, since a dual-stack Service appears in both

kubeproxy_partial_restore_failures_24h.why: Partial iptables-restore failures over 24h per node (a partial sync that fell back to a full one). Added to kubeproxy_restore_failures_24h by lib/kubeproxy.py. Empty when no failure happened (1.33 and later) and in ipvs and nftables mode, where the counter is not registered

kubeproxy_programming_p99_1h.why: p99 seconds from a Service/Endpoint change reaching the apiserver until it is programmed into node rules (NaN when there were no changes)

kubeproxy_rest_client_errors_1h.why: Non-2xx responses from kube-proxy → apiserver calls (1h, EKS job)

kubeproxy_restore_failures_24h.why: Full iptables-restore failures over 24h per node. Must be 0. On failure that node keeps stale Service routing. Empty when no failure happened (1.33 and later) or in nftables mode

kubeproxy_rules_pending_s.why: Last queued change time minus last sync time (seconds). Positive and above 60s means a change has not reached the node yet (stale rules)

kubeproxy_sync_p99_1h.why: p99 seconds of a rule sync (one iptables-restore). Above 1s Service/Endpoint changes reach nodes slowly; above 5s the iptables rule count is at its limit

kubeproxy_sync_p99_by_instance_1h.why: Sync p99 per node. If only one node is slow it is that node's rule count or CPU

kubeproxy_syncs_1h.why: Sync count per node over 1h. Runs on every change and every syncPeriod

kubeproxy_targets.why: Scrape target status for job=kube-proxy (EKS). Empty on k3s, which has no such job

large_request_containers.why: Containers whose CPU or memory request exceeds half the median node allocatable. Workloads that defeat bin packing and make Karpenter launch big nodes. The median rather than the smallest node is used because a 1-core smallest node would flag every 0.5-core request

localpath_fs_avail_ratio.why: Free ratio of the node root filesystem. local-path volumes have no capacity enforcement (capacity is nominal), so when this fills up kubelet eviction and k3s SQLite write failures come together

localpath_fs_growth_bytes_per_day.why: 7-day trend of root filesystem usage (bytes/day, deriv). If positive, the days until full can be computed

memory_limit_p95_ratio_7d.why: Container 7-day memory p95 / limit. Above 0.9 is on the verge of OOMKilled

memory_p95_7d_bytes.why: Container 7-day memory working set p95 absolute value (bytes). Evidence number for the ratio checks

memory_request_p95_ratio_7d.why: Container 7-day memory working set p95 / request. Below 0.3 is over-allocation; only requests >= 256Mi and pods older than 1 day

monitoring_oomkilled.why: Containers in the monitoring namespace whose last termination reason was OOMKilled

monitoring_restarts_7d.why: Restarts per pod in the monitoring namespace over 7d (instability of the stack itself)

namespace_cpu_max_7d.why: Namespace 7-day CPU max (15-minute samples). A large multiple of p95 means a bursty tenant (CI runners, batch)

namespace_cpu_median_7d.why: Namespace 7-day CPU median. The denominator of the burst multiple (max/median)

namespace_cpu_p95_7d.why: Namespace (tenant) 7-day CPU p95 (cores). Baseline for comparing tenant usage and noisy-neighbour candidates

namespace_cpu_throttled_ratio_7d.why: 7-day CPU throttled-period ratio per namespace. A production tenant throttled on a shared node has either a low limit or a neighbour eating CPU

namespace_memory_p95_7d_bytes.why: Namespace 7-day memory working set p95 (bytes). How much a tenant without a quota actually uses

namespace_node_cpu_share_p95_7d.why: Per node, what share of allocatable CPU each namespace uses (7-day p95). When one tenant dominates a node, the other tenants on it get squeezed

node_boot_time.why: Node boot time. Tracks recent reboots and node replacements

node_cpu_request_ratio.why: Sum of CPU requests / allocatable per node. Near 1 nothing more can be scheduled; a large gap from actual usage means over-requesting

node_cpu_saturated_minutes_7d.why: Minutes the node CPU usage exceeded 90% of allocatable (7d, 5-minute samples). At 0 a noisy neighbour had no room to do real harm

node_cpu_usage_ratio_5m.why: Actual CPU usage / allocatable per node. Next to the request ratio it shows over- and under-requesting

node_cpu_usage_ratio_p95_7d.why: Node 7-day CPU usage p95 / allocatable. Used instead of the 5-minute instant value to judge the request gap (current nodes only)

node_memory_available_ratio.why: Node MemAvailable / MemTotal. The real headroom including usage outside containers (kernel, cache, host processes)

node_memory_request_ratio.why: Sum of memory requests / allocatable per node

node_memory_usage_ratio.why: Actual memory working set / allocatable per node

node_memory_usage_ratio_p95_7d.why: Node 7-day memory working set p95 / allocatable (current nodes only)

node_network_errors_1d.why: RX/TX errors on physical NICs over 24h (per node and device, virtual interfaces excluded). Non-zero means NIC, driver, cable or ENA trouble

node_network_errors_5m.why: NIC receive errors and transmit drops. Non-zero means driver, MTU or overlay trouble

node_pvc_pods_count.why: Pods using a PVC per node (≈ attached volumes). Compared with the CSINode attach limit

node_swap_total_bytes.why: Swap size. If not 0, check the kubelet settings (failSwapOn, swapBehavior)

node_tcp_timewait.why: TIME_WAIT socket count per node. The early signal before SNAT source ports (about 28,000 by default) are exhausted by a flood of short connections (Prezi case)

nodes_seen_1d.why: Every node-exporter instance seen in the last 24 hours with its node name and the time of its last sample. A node here but not in inventory.json left the cluster within the window; its remaining series are not judged by the node checks and the summary lists it under nodes.gone_24h

ntp_offset_seconds.why: Clock offset (seconds). Above 0.1 TLS, tokens and distributed log timestamps drift

ntp_sync_status.why: Clock sync status (1 = synced). At 0 check chrony or systemd-timesyncd

oom_events_7d.why: How many times a container was OOM-killed in 7 days (increase of cAdvisor container_oom_events_total). "Last termination reason" shows only one event; this is the frequency

oom_pods_7d.why: Every container that ended with OOMKilled at any time in 7 days and restarted in the window, including pods a rollout has since replaced, with the 7-day restart increase of that pod; a pod whose last OOM is older than the window keeps the reason label but has no restart in it and is left out. resources.oomkilled-repeated counts a workload's OOM history from this, not from the pods alive at collection time

oomkilled_last_terminated.why: Containers whose last termination reason was OOMKilled. Memory limit too small or a leak

pdb_disruptions_allowed.why: Allowed disruptions per PDB. At 0 drains and upgrades are blocked by that PDB

pod_info_7d.why: uid, node and owner of the pods in oom_pods_7d, replaced ones included. The kernel's oom-kill line names the pod by uid, and this is how a uid of a pod that no longer exists is mapped back to its workload

pod_network_rx_bytes_1h.why: 1h average received bytes/s per pod (above 1KB/s). Large variance between pods of one workload means keep-alive or gRPC pinning traffic to one pod. lib/traffic.py groups by workload

pod_pending_seconds.why: Seconds since creation for pods Pending right now. Only above 60s. A sign that the node autoscaler is not making room

pod_ready_ratio_24h.why: Share of the last 24h a currently Running pod was Ready (below 0.99 only). Time it was out of the endpoints due to readiness failures. Pairs with Unhealthy events

pods_pending.why: Pending pods. A sign of unschedulability (resources, taints, affinity, PVC)

pods_waiting_reason.why: Waiting reasons such as CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerConfigError

prom_compactions_failed_7d.why: TSDB compaction failures (7d). The first sign of disk shortage or corruption

prom_head_series.why: Active series in memory. Above 1M, memory and rule evaluation both slow down (a small cluster is typically 100-200k)

prom_notifications_dropped_1d.why: Alerts dropped from the Prometheus → Alertmanager queue overflow (24h). Anything above 0 means alerts were lost

prom_notifications_errors_1d.why: Alerts that failed to send to Alertmanager (24h, per Alertmanager address)

prom_oldest_sample_days.why: Age in days of the oldest sample actually left in the TSDB. Much shorter than retention means data was cut by disk shortage or a reinstall

prom_oomkilled.why: Whether the Prometheus container's last termination reason was OOMKilled (kube-state-metrics)

prom_pvc_used_ratio.why: Prometheus data PVC usage ratio (kubelet volume stats — not available for local volumes such as local-path)

prom_reload_ok.why: Whether the last config reload succeeded (0 means new rules/scrape config were not applied and the old config is still running)

prom_replicas.why: Number of Prometheus instances whose own metrics are scraped (one prometheus_build_info series each)

prom_retention_days.why: Configured retention (seconds → days). With retention.size at 0 only time is enforced, so the disk can fill first

prom_rss_vs_limit.why: Prometheus container RSS ÷ memory limit. Above 0.85 the next compaction or large query gets OOMKilled

prom_rule_eval_ratio_top.why: Top rule groups by evaluation duration ÷ interval. Near 1, evaluations fall behind and alerts are late or skipped

prom_rule_iterations_missed_1d.why: Rule evaluations skipped for overrunning the interval (24h)

prom_sample_limit_exceeded_1h.why: Scrapes dropped entirely for exceeding sampleLimit over 1h, summed over every target. Which targets are failing on it comes from prometheus/targets.json

prom_scrape_interval_s.why: Longest scrape interval in use (seconds): the median interval length of the longest configured interval. Fallback denominator for the slow-scrape judgement when prometheus/targets.json is missing

prom_scrape_slow_jobs.why: Max scrape duration per job (seconds). Above half the scrape interval (usually 30s) the target is slow or its response too large

prometheus_remote_write_failed_1h.why: Failed remote-write samples (when configured). The path to long-term storage is broken

prometheus_scrape_samples_top.why: Top targets by samples per scrape. Finding the cardinality culprit

prometheus_storage_bytes.why: TSDB disk usage plus WAL. Compare with the PVC size

prometheus_tsdb_head_series.why: Active series count. The first indicator of a cardinality explosion

pvc_available_bytes.why: PVC bytes remaining. Together with the growth rate, for the "full in N days" estimate

pvc_capacity_bytes.why: PVC capacity (bytes). Evidence number for the usage check

pvc_growth_bytes_per_day_7d.why: Daily growth in bytes from a 7-day linear regression (deriv). Negative means shrinking

pvc_inode_ratio.why: PVC inode usage. Volumes with many small files (cache, logs) run out of inodes before space

pvc_usage_ratio.why: PVC usage (kubelet_volume_stats). Above 0.85 a database is about to fail writes

qos_class_counts.why: Pod count per QoS class. BestEffort pods in production die first under node pressure

restarts_24h.why: Top restart counts over 24h. A combined signal of CrashLoop, OOM and probe failures

restarts_7d.why: Top restart counts over 7d. Intermittent restarts do not show in a 24h window

rule_evaluation_failures.why: Rule groups whose evaluation failed (syntax, missing metric). A failing rule is a rule that never fires

rule_group_duration_top.why: Slowest rule groups. If evaluation exceeds the interval, alerts are late or skipped

saturation_metric_namespaces.why: Namespaces with saturation metrics (queue length, connection pool, thread pool, in-flight). The golden signal most often missing

scrape_targets_down_by_job.why: Targets with up==0 per job. A ServiceMonitor exists but the scrape fails

secret_types.why: Secret type (kube_secret_type). service-account-token and helm release Secrets are excluded from the orphan check

secrets_by_name.why: Secret names and namespaces (kube_secret_info, no values). For finding Secrets nobody references (orphans)

secrets_meta.why: Secret count per namespace (kube_secret_info). Secret values are never fetched; only metadata via metrics

targets_down.why: Failed scrape targets (up==0). What Prometheus cannot see, no metric check can see

unhealthy.name: app-c-coturn
unhealthy.message: Deployment does not have minimum availability.

alerts.note: always_firing = 7-day sample count at or above 95% of Watchdog (always firing). On EKS, KubeControllerManagerDown and KubeSchedulerDown fire forever because the control plane is invisible — false positives

matrix.symptom: pods die and requests fail or slow down
part or all of a service is down
every pod on that node stops

uncovered.symptom: pods die and requests fail or slow down

controlplane.skip_reason: no k3s server journal read (logs/node/<node>/ missing: no node access)

controller_manager.note: k3s runs as one process, so controller-manager errors are mixed into nodes[<server>].errors_by_count

gaps: k3s-platform.txt missing (node access failed or step not run)
k3s-platform.txt missing (node access failed or step not run)

datastore.note: The slow request log is journalctl -u k3s warn lines over 24 hours, sampled 15 lines per hour (hours_saturated = hours that had more, hours_with_warn = number of hours with any warn — if they cluster around the kubegap collection time, it is our own load). etcd expects apply within 100ms. DB size is du of /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/db

node-a: k3s-platform.txt missing (node access failed or step not run)
node-b: k3s-platform.txt missing (node access failed or step not run)

logs.component_logs: counted while they were collected; no line is stored

signatures.name: MetalLB speaker errors
signatures.meaning: ARP/BGP announcement of the external IP failed, so it is unreachable from outside. `failed to announce service` (speaker), `failed to send ARP reply` (also used for NDP), `failed to send BGP update|withdraw|keepalive` are the named lines; the first alternative counts every other error-level line of the speaker and controller pods except `partial join`.
signatures.cause: Interface selection, L2Advertisement settings, node network.
signatures.verify: kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker --since=1h | grep '"level":"error"' | grep -v 'partial join' | head

signatures.name: fluent-bit chunk flush failed
signatures.pattern: failed to flush chunk|could not flush|HTTP status=(4|5)\d\d
signatures.meaning: Logs are not being written to the output (Elasticsearch, Loki, CloudWatch) and are retrying. Past the retry limit they are dropped. The lines are "[ warn] [engine] failed to flush chunk '...', retry in N seconds" (one per retry) and the output plugin's "[error] ... HTTP status=NNN URI=..." or "could not flush records to host:port"; the HTTP response body follows on its own lines.
signatures.cause: Output target down or rejecting (ES disk watermark, mapping conflict), authentication, network.
signatures.verify: kubectl logs -n <ns> -l app.kubernetes.io/name=fluent-bit --since=1h | grep -c 'failed to flush'

signatures.name: fluent-bit cannot connect to its output
signatures.pattern: no upstream connections available|upstream connection initialization error|[Cc]onnection refused|[Cc]onnection timed out|connection #\d+ to \S+ timed out|broken connection
signatures.meaning: The connection to the output target itself fails. Logs pile up in the memory/file buffer and are eventually dropped. The lines are "[error] [output:...] no upstream connections available", "[error] [src/flb_...c:NNN errno=111] Connection refused" (glibc wording), "[upstream] connection #N to host:port timed out after N seconds" and "[http_client] broken connection to host:port ?".
signatures.cause: Elasticsearch or Loki down, changed Service name/port, network policy.

signatures.name: ACME challenge validation failed
signatures.pattern: propagation check failed|error (getting solver for|cleaning up|accepting) challenge|error waiting for authorization
signatures.meaning: Proof of domain ownership is not passing. Issuance is delayed. Up to 1.20.x the challenge controller logs `propagation check failed` on every self-check; from 1.21.0 the propagation wait is only a V(4) line and the Challenge status reason (`Waiting for HTTP-01 challenge propagation`, read by the verify command), so only the solver, cleanup, accept and authorization errors remain in the log.
signatures.cause: DNS record propagation delay, ingress not serving the .well-known path, firewall.

signatures.name: MetalLB speaker cannot reach a peer speaker
signatures.meaning: A speaker pod that the API server still lists is not reachable on port 7946, so the memberlist join to it times out. The speaker retries once a minute and logs this at level error each time; the speakers that are up keep announcing. It means a node is down (its speaker pod stays listed until evicted) or the memberlist port is blocked between nodes.
signatures.cause: Node NotReady or powered off, a firewall or NetworkPolicy blocking TCP/UDP 7946 between nodes.
signatures.verify: kubectl get nodes; kubectl get pods -n metallb-system -l component=speaker -o wide; kubectl logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker --since=1h | grep -c 'partial join'

signatures.name: TLS Secret without an owning Certificate (not managed by cert-manager)
signatures.pattern: unable to fetch certificate that owns the secret.*not found
signatures.meaning: A TLS Secret carries cert-manager annotations but its Certificate resource is gone. An Ingress may be serving a certificate that will never renew (discovered at expiry). The cainjector prints the line on every event of such a Secret, so the count is events, not Secrets; the verify command lists the Secrets.
signatures.cause: Certificate deleted but Secret left behind, a namespace move, a hand-made Secret.
signatures.verify: kubectl get secrets -A --field-selector type=kubernetes.io/tls -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.metadata.annotations["cert-manager.io/certificate-name"]) | .metadata.namespace+"/"+.metadata.name' ; kubectl get certificates -A

signatures.name: Repeated Grafana login failures
signatures.pattern: Failed to authenticate|API key is invalid|invalid API key
signatures.meaning: Many wrong passwords may mean a publicly exposed Grafana is being brute-forced. The line is the Info "Failed to authenticate request" client=auth.client.form error="[password-auth.failed] failed to authenticate identity: ..." (Unauthorized errors log at Info); API-key failures carry "[api-key.invalid] API key is invalid".
signatures.cause: Internet exposure plus default accounts, automation using an expired API key.

namespaces.classification_rule: prod=inventory prod_like, dev=dev_like, ci=name (runner, ci, jenkins, tekton, ...) or a namespace with a runner CR, system=kube-* plus detected component namespaces, other=everything else

noisy.note: The noisy-neighbour verdict is left to the LLM (type: llm, tenancy.noisy-neighbor). If node saturation minutes are 0, no neighbour could have done harm. Only nodes where a dominant namespace, saturation and prod throttling on the same node overlap are candidates.

ndots.note: With the default ndots:5, an external name with fewer than 5 dots (api.example.com) is first tried with <ns>.svc.cluster.local, svc.cluster.local, cluster.local and the VPC search domain appended, producing 3-4 NXDOMAINs before the real name is asked. That is why the NXDOMAIN ratio is high and the query count is several times the number of real names. Fixes: trailing dot (FQDN), ndots:2, or the autopath plugin

config.source: none (embedded in k3s — only changeable via --kube-proxy-arg)

kubeproxy.note: On k3s, kube-proxy runs inside the k3s process, so there is no DaemonSet or ConfigMap and its metrics appear mixed into the kubelet scrape (instance :10250, :6443). rules_pending_s = queue time − sync time (0 if negative). iptables_rules is 'the number of rules written in the last sync', so after a partial sync (seen on EKS 1.32: nat 5) it is not the full scale — judge scale by services and endpoints

kedactl.note: Secret existence is judged by name only via kube_secret_info (no values). Operator metrics are empty when --enable-prometheus-metrics=false

esoctl.note: Secret values are not read. stale = Ready items whose refreshTime is older than 3× refreshInterval (minimum 1 hour). Metrics are cumulative since the process started

argocdctl.note: Metrics are cumulative since each process started. Git credentials and Secret values are not read. prod = destination namespace or a managed resource's namespace is prod_like

flannel.note: Node data (mtu, vxlan, cumulative counters, sysctl) comes from the k3s-platform node script's flannel section (SSH). 24-hour increases come from node-exporter. The vxlan backend is unencrypted; if nodes span different subnets or a public network, the wireguard-native backend is the right choice

local_path.note: local-path volumes are plain directories, so PVC capacity is not a limit (du usage can exceed it). Directory usage and orphan directories come from the node script's (SSH) du list (top 30). Filesystem free space comes from node-exporter

l2.note: In L2 mode one node advertises each service IP. If a single node advertises every IP, its NIC receives all external traffic, and when it dies everything is cut off during failover (about 10 seconds). Intended if pinned with nodeSelectors
